cards.definition: Saturday and Sunday, when most people do not work.
cards.example:
- How was your weekend? Did you relax a little?
Como foi seu fim de semana? Descansou um pouco?
cards.note: AmE: on the weekend; BrE: at the weekend.

cards.definition: The condition of the air outside: sun, rain, wind, temperature.
cards.example:
- The weather is crazy today — sun, rain, sun again.
O tempo está maluco hoje — sol, chuva, sol de novo.
cards.note: Clima de um lugar (padrão do ano) = climate.

cards.definition: The cars and buses moving on the roads.
cards.example:
- The traffic was terrible this morning — forty minutes on Paulista.
O trânsito estava terrível hoje de manhã — quarenta minutos na Paulista.

cards.definition: The things you have decided to do in the future.
cards.example:
- Any plans for tonight?
Algum plano para hoje à noite?
cards.note: Any plans for…? é a pergunta social padrão de sexta-feira.

cards.definition: A day when people do not work, usually for a national celebration.
cards.example:
- Thursday is a holiday, so the office will be quiet on Friday.
Quinta é feriado, então o escritório vai estar vazio na sexta.
cards.note: AmE: férias = vacation; BrE usa holiday para férias também.

cards.definition: To meet someone and share news after some time apart.
cards.example:
- Let’s catch up over coffee — it has been a month!
Vamos pôr o papo em dia num café — já faz um mês!
cards.note: Catch up on work = pôr o trabalho em dia.

cards.translation: como vão as coisas? e aí?
cards.definition: A friendly, informal way of asking how someone is.
cards.example:
- — How’s it going? — Pretty good! Busy week, though.
— E aí, como vai? — Tudo certo! Semana corrida, mas bem.
cards.note: Resposta curta e positiva (pretty good), não um relatório da vida.

cards.definition: A friendly phrase used when you meet someone after a long time.
cards.example:
- Long time no see! How have you been?
Quanto tempo! Como você tem passado?
cards.note: Expressão fixa e informal — universal em qualquer escritório.

cards.example:
- My parents visit us every holiday.
Meus pais nos visitam em todo feriado.
cards.note: “Parentes” = relatives. My parents = meus pais, só os dois.

cards.definition: Special clothes worn to look like someone or something else.
cards.example:
- Nice costume! Was the party fun?
Que fantasia legal! A festa foi boa?

questions.prompt: Which one is correct in American English?
questions.explanation: “On the weekend” (US) or “at the weekend” (UK). “In” comes from the Portuguese “no”.

questions.prompt: You want a description of today's conditions outside. You ask:
questions.explanation: “What's it like?” is how English asks for a description.

questions.prompt: The _____ was terrible this morning — forty minutes on Paulista.
questions.explanation: “Traffic” is uncountable: no “a traffic”, no “traffics”, singular verb.
In this expression the word is always plural.

questions.prompt: Quinta é feriado, então a sexta vai ser vazia no escritório.
questions.answer: Thursday is a holiday, so the office will be quiet on Friday.|Thursday is a holiday, so Friday will be quiet at the office.
questions.explanation: “A holiday” is countable here: one specific day off.

questions.prompt: Let's _____ over coffee — it has been a month!
questions.explanation: “Catch up OVER coffee”: “over” is the preposition for doing something while eating or drinking.
Informal and very common; the expected answer is short.

questions.prompt: You meet a colleague you have not seen for a year. You say:
questions.explanation: A fixed phrase — it breaks grammar on purpose and cannot be changed.

questions.prompt: You mean your uncles, cousins and grandparents. You say:
questions.explanation: “Parents” is only mother and father. The Portuguese “parentes” is “relatives”.

questions.prompt: You wear a suit and tie to the office. You wear a…
questions.explanation: “Costume” is a party or theatre outfit. The Portuguese “costume” (habit) is “custom”.
